opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is simply the cost of formalization itself. Translating a mathematical statement from natural language into Lean is much harder than people expect. A human mathematician reading a paper fills in an enormous amount of implicit context: conventions, notation, "obvious" lemmas, the standard way a field sets things up. Lean doesn't let you skip any of that. So even stating a problem correctly, before you prove anything, can take real expertise. And if the statement is subtly wrong, with a missing hypothesis or an off-by-one in an index, you can end up proving something trivial or something different from what you meant. Getting the statement faithful is one of the most underrated bottlenecks.

The second is library coverage. Mathlib is remarkable, and the community has done heroic work, but it's still uneven. Some areas, like algebra and parts of analysis and topology, are quite mature. Others, like big chunks of combinatorics, probability, or more applied and research-level areas, are much thinner. When you go to formalize a problem in one of those areas, you often find you first have to build the basic definitions and API yourself. That's a huge tax.

The third is the gap between how humans reason and how proofs have to be written for the kernel. A human proof says "by symmetry," or "a standard compactness argument." In Lean, each of those steps can turn into dozens or hundreds of lines. Automation helps, but tactics are still brittle, and proofs break when the library changes underneath them. Maintenance is a real cost.

Then there's the data problem, which matters a lot for AI. Compared with natural-language math, there's very little formal math in the world. For training models, that scarcity is a fundamental constraint. You can't just scrape the internet for Lean proofs the way you can for text. That's partly why autoformalization, getting models to translate informal math into formal statements and proofs, is such an important direction. It's a way to bootstrap more data. But it runs straight back into the first problem: how do you know the translation is faithful?

And finally there's a human and community side. The number of people who are fluent both in serious mathematics and in Lean is still small. Mathematicians mostly aren't trained in it, and it can feel like a detour from "real" research. So adoption depends on making the tools feel genuinely useful to working mathematicians, not just a verification burden at the end.

What makes me optimistic is that these obstacles are exactly where AI can help. Models can draft formal statements, fill in tedious steps, search the library, and repair broken proofs, while Lean acts as the ground truth that keeps them honest. You get a really nice loop: the AI provides creativity and scale, and the formal system provides verification. I think that combination is what will eventually make formalization cheap enough to become the default rather than the exception.

r001.rationale: The response says that thin Mathlib coverage can force formalizers to build definitions and APIs themselves, but it does not identify machines’ difficulty constructing those missing definitions as the obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are really a few layers to it, and they're quite different in nature.

The first is what I'd call the translation gap, or autoformalization. Most of mathematics lives in natural language, in papers and textbooks, and the statements are often informal in ways we don't even notice. A paper might say "for sufficiently large n" or "with the usual conventions," and a human reader fills that in instantly. When you try to write that as a Lean statement, you have to make every assumption explicit, and it's very easy to write something that type-checks but is subtly not the theorem you meant. It could be trivially true, or vacuously true because a hypothesis is unsatisfiable. So just getting the statement right, before you even think about the proof, is a real bottleneck, and verifying that a formal statement faithfully captures an informal one is itself not something Lean can check for you.

The second obstacle is the library. Lean is only as powerful as Mathlib, and Mathlib is incredible, it's one of the largest coherent bodies of formalized mathematics ever built, but it's still uneven. Some areas like algebra and basic analysis are very well covered. Other areas, especially more recent research-level mathematics, or anything that depends on a big technical machine, just aren't there yet. So when you want to formalize a modern result, you often find that eighty percent of the work is building the prerequisites, not proving the theorem itself. And the definitions you choose matter enormously. If you pick a definition that's convenient for one proof but doesn't match how Mathlib structures things, you'll pay for that for a long time.

The third is the proof search itself. Even when the statement is right and the library has what you need, the gap between a human proof and a formal proof is huge. A line in a paper that says "by a standard compactness argument" might be hundreds of lines of Lean. And a lot of that is not deep mathematics, it's bookkeeping, coercions between types, rewriting things into the exact form a lemma expects. That's where automation and AI can help a lot, but it's also where current systems still struggle, because the search space is enormous and the signal for whether you're on the right track is very sparse. You don't get partial credit from the kernel.

And then there's the human side, which I think people underestimate. Lean has a steep learning curve, and the community of people who are both strong mathematicians and fluent in Lean is still small. Mathematicians don't yet have strong incentives to formalize their work, because it takes much longer than writing the paper and the reward structure of academia doesn't recognize it. So the real question for me is less "can we formalize this" and more "how do we make it cheap enough that it becomes the default." That's really where I think the interesting work is happening now, using models to close the gap so that formalization becomes something you do alongside the mathematics, rather than a separate heroic project afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says Mathlib lacks some prerequisites and that building them can take most of the work, but it does not identify machines’ difficulty constructing definitions absent from Mathlib.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different bottlenecks. The first is translating an informal mathematical statement into a precise formal statement. On paper, we leave a lot implicit—assumptions, conventions, even what objects we’re working with. In Lean, you have to make those things precise. And you have to check that the statement you formalized actually captures the problem you intended to solve.

The second is the supporting infrastructure. A proof might say, “This follows from a standard theorem,” but you need that theorem available in the library, in a form that applies to your situation. Sometimes a very short mathematical argument requires a substantial amount of groundwork.

Then there’s finding the proof itself. Lean checks each step rigorously, but that doesn’t mean it automatically knows which lemma to use or which intermediate claim will make the argument work. That search can be difficult for both people and AI systems.

So I’d distinguish verification from formalization and proof discovery. Once you have a complete proof, checking it is the part Lean is designed to handle. Getting from the informal problem to that complete proof is where much of the difficulty lies.

r001.rationale: The response mentions library support and proof-search difficulty for people and AI, but does not identify machines’ difficulty constructing definitions that are absent from mathlib.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two main challenges. One is translating an informal mathematical statement into a precise formal statement. On paper, we leave a lot implicit: assumptions, definitions, even what we mean by two objects being equivalent. In Lean, those choices have to be explicit. And you have to check that the statement you formalized actually captures the problem you intended to solve.

The second challenge is constructing the proof. A step that a mathematician considers obvious might require substantial work in Lean, especially if the relevant background theory hasn’t been formalized yet. If it has, you still need to find the right results in the library and understand how to use them.

So I’d distinguish checking a proof from finding and expressing one. Lean can check a completed proof, but getting to that point—bridging informal reasoning and the formal language—is where much of the difficulty lies.

r001.rationale: The response says missing formalized background theory can make proving difficult, but does not identify machines’ difficulty constructing definitions absent from mathlib.
